title: India Confronts Pakistan at UN, Highlights Rights Suppression in Occupied Kashmir
excerpt: From the UNHRC to the Security Council, Indian diplomats have mounted a sustained offensive against Islamabad's record on human rights in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, accusing it of meeting civilian demands with bullets.
body:
• India's Ambassador Parvathaneni Harish rebuked Pakistan at a UNSC debate on July 22, calling Islamabad's Kashmir references a misuse of UN platforms and linking the Indus Waters Treaty to cross-border terrorism.
  • At the 62nd UNHRC session in June, Indian diplomat Anupama Singh accused Pakistan of a brutal crackdown in Rawalakot, where security forces fired on protesters demanding basic rights.
  • New Delhi has called out Pakistan's record at the UNSC, UNGA, and UNHRC in 2026, referencing the Kabul airstrike and 1971 atrocities while reaffirming that Jammu and Kashmir is an integral part of India.

India Fires Back After Pakistan Raises Kashmir at UNSC

India's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Parvathaneni Harish, delivered a sharp rebuke to Pakistan on July 22 during a UN Security Council high-level open debate on natural resources governance. Islamabad had raised the issue of Jammu and Kashmir during the session, prompting Harish to respond that India had not intended to bring bilateral matters into the debate but was compelled to act.

https://x.com/PTI_News/status/2080471399958020403

Harish accused Pakistan of misusing the UN platform to push what he called a false narrative. He reaffirmed that Jammu and Kashmir "has always been, is, and will remain an integral and inalienable part of India," adding that the only unresolved issue concerns Pakistan's illegal occupation of Indian territory.

The Indian envoy tied the exchange to the Indus Waters Treaty, stating that cooperation built on trust cannot function when cross-border terrorism is used as an instrument of state policy, according to The Impressive Times.

Rawalakot Crackdown Brought to UNHRC Floor

The UNSC exchange was the latest in a string of confrontations. A month earlier, at the 62nd session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva on June 19, First Secretary Anupama Singh exercised India's right of reply after Pakistan and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation referenced Jammu and Kashmir.

"Demands for bread were met with bullets and brutality."

— Anupama Singh, First Secretary, Permanent Mission of India to the UN

Singh drew attention to a security crackdown in Rawalakot, a town in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK). According to the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKJAAC), Pakistani security forces dispersed protesters on June 7 and June 14, killing at least two people and injuring several others. Communication services were disrupted, and restrictions on food supplies worsened shortages.

Singh accused Pakistan of decades of military land grabs, demographic engineering, and denial of basic freedoms in PoJK. She described Pakistan as a "Frankenstein State" that nurtures terrorism and now faces its own consequences.

A Broader Pattern at the UN

At a UNGA plenary on June 5, Harish told Pakistan that the Security Council seat it holds as a non-permanent member "is not a forum for peddling biased and false narratives." Pakistan's tenure on the Council ends later this year.

During a separate UNSC debate on the protection of civilians, Harish cited Pakistan's airstrike on the Omid Addiction Treatment Hospital in Kabul during Ramadan in March 2026. The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan confirmed the attack killed 269 civilians and injured 122 others. Amnesty International, in a report released on July 22, found no evidence to support Pakistan's claim it targeted military infrastructure, calling the strike a "possible war crime."

"The world has not forgotten that it was during the holy month of Ramadan... at a time of peace, reflection, and mercy, that Pakistan conducted a barbaric airstrike."

— Parvathaneni Harish, India's Permanent Representative to the UN

Protests and Pressure on PoJK

Outside the council chambers, the United Kashmir People's National Party staged a protest at the Broken Chair monument outside the UN in Geneva, demanding an independent international investigation into the Rawalakot killings. The JKJAAC has alleged that Pakistani authorities imposed communication blackouts and movement restrictions to suppress protests across PoJK.

What's Next

Pakistan's non-permanent UNSC seat expires at the end of 2026, which could reduce its ability to raise Kashmir in that forum. India has renewed its push for Council reform, proposing an expansion to 25 or 26 members — a campaign backed by Brazil, Germany, and Japan.

India's strategy of turning Pakistan's own record back on it — from PoJK repression to the Kabul airstrike — signals that New Delhi intends to remain on the offensive at every UN platform.
